questions.statement: Choose the correct option: 'I ___ (call) you as soon as I arrive.'
questions.context: A student explains a plan to a friend in San Salvador, SV.

options.feedback: 'Will call' is the future simple: 'will' plus the base form 'call' with no change in spelling.
'Am calling' is the present continuous, which describes an action happening now rather than a promise.
'Called' is the past simple and would describe an action that already happened.
'Would' needs the base form of the verb after it, so 'would called' is not correct.

questions.explanation: The verb 'will' plus the base form of the verb forms the future simple, so the blank needs 'call' with no -ing ending and no auxiliary before it.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the correct option: 'It ___ rain tomorrow afternoon.'
questions.context: A weather forecast read before class in San Salvador, SV.

options.feedback: 'Is raining' is the present continuous and describes rain happening at the moment of speaking.
'Will rain' is the future simple, and it is the natural way to predict tomorrow's weather.
'Rained' is the past simple and cannot predict an afternoon that has not arrived.
'Rains' is the present simple used for repeated patterns, not for a single future event.

questions.explanation: A prediction about tomorrow uses the future simple 'will' plus the base form, and the subject 'it' carries no auxiliary of its own.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What does the future simple express?
questions.context: A grammar explanation given in an English class in San Salvador, SV.

options.text: An action that is happening at this moment
options.feedback: An action in progress right now belongs to the present continuous, not to 'will'.

options.text: A habit that started in the past
options.feedback: 'Will' points forward, while habits connected to the past need the past continuous.

options.text: A decision or prediction about the future
options.feedback: 'Will' covers predictions and spontaneous decisions, which are its two main uses.

options.text: A sequence of past events in order
options.feedback: Narrating past events in order uses the past simple, not the future simple.

questions.explanation: The future simple with 'will' is used for predictions, promises, decisions made at the moment of speaking and offers of help.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the correct offer: 'You look tired. I ___ help you.'
questions.context: A classmate offers help during a group project in San Salvador, SV.

options.feedback: 'Am helping' is the present continuous, which describes help already in progress.
'Would' must be followed by the base form, never by the -ing form of the verb.
'Helped' is the past simple and cannot express an offer for the future.
'I will help you' is a spontaneous offer decided at the moment of speaking.

questions.explanation: An offer of help made at the moment of speaking uses 'will' plus the base form of the verb.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the correct option: 'Look at those clouds! It ___ snow.'
questions.context: Students watching the sky from a school yard in San Salvador, SV.

options.feedback: 'Is snowing' describes snow already falling at the moment of speaking.
'Snows' is the present simple, which describes a regular pattern rather than a prediction.
'Snowed' is the past simple and describes an event that has already finished.
A prediction based on what the speaker sees at that moment uses 'will' plus the base form.

questions.explanation: The speaker makes a prediction about the immediate future, and 'will' plus the base form is the standard way to express it.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which verb follows 'will'?
questions.context: A quick drill in a school in Santa Tecla, SV.

options.feedback: 'Arriving' is the -ing form, which belongs with 'am', 'is' or 'are', not with 'will'.
'Arrived' is the past simple form and cannot follow the auxiliary 'will'.
'Will arrive' joins the auxiliary with the base form, which is the correct combination.
'Arrives' is the third person present simple, a form 'will' does not take.

questions.explanation: 'Will' is an auxiliary verb, so it is always followed by the base form of the main verb without any inflection.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the correct option: 'We ___ meet at the library at four.'
questions.context: A study group agrees on a plan in a school in San Salvador, SV.

options.feedback: 'Met' is the past simple and would state that the meeting already happened.
'Will meet' presents the meeting as a future arrangement made now.
'Are meeting' is the present continuous and describes a meeting in progress now.
'Would' must be followed by the base form 'meet', so 'would met' is ungrammatical.

questions.explanation: The group is arranging a future meeting decided in the conversation, so 'will' plus the base form is correct.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the correct option: 'He probably ___ (not / come) to the party.'
questions.context: A discussion about weekend plans in a school in San Salvador, SV.

options.feedback: 'Will not' plus the base form builds the negative future simple correctly.
'Will' takes the base form, so the -ing form 'coming' cannot follow it.
'Does not come' is the present simple negative and describes a habit.
'Did not come' is the past simple negative and refers to a finished action.

questions.explanation: A negative prediction about the future uses 'will not' plus the base form, and 'not' comes right after 'will'.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the correct contraction: 'I will not be late.'
questions.context: A message written before a school event in San Salvador, SV.

options.feedback: 'Wll' drops letters without an apostrophe and loses the meaning of the negative.
'Will not' shortens to "won't", with an apostrophe standing in for the missing 'll'.
'Am not' is the present continuous negative and describes a current state.
'Do not' builds the negative of the present simple, not of the future.

questions.explanation: 'Will not' contracts to "won't" in English, so the sentence becomes "I won't be late".
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the correct sentence.
questions.context: A test on future forms in a secondary school in San Salvador, SV.

options.text: I will sending the report tonight.
options.feedback: 'Will' never takes the -ing form, so 'will sending' is ungrammatical.

options.text: I am will sending the report tonight.
options.feedback: Two auxiliaries cannot govern the same main verb in English, so this is impossible.

options.text: I will sends the report tonight.
options.feedback: 'Sends' is the third person present simple and does not follow 'will'.

options.text: I will send the report tonight.
options.feedback: 'Will send' is the future simple: auxiliary 'will' followed by the base form 'send'.

questions.explanation: Only the sentence built with 'will' plus the base form of the verb is a correct future simple.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the correct option: 'They ___ (not / know) what to do, so they will ask the teacher.'
questions.context: A discussion about an unfamiliar task in a school in San Salvador, SV.

options.feedback: 'Did not know' is the past simple negative and describes a finished situation.
'Will not know' would add a second future clause and would not match the present explanation.
'Do not know' is the present simple negative and explains a situation that holds now.
English places the negation after the auxiliary 'do', never at the start like this.

questions.explanation: The reason clause states a present situation, so the present simple negative 'do not know' fits before the future clause.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the correct future form: 'By next June, she ___ (finish) her degree.'
questions.context: An academic planning conversation in a school in San Salvador, SV.

options.feedback: 'Will have finished' is the future perfect, which places the action before a future deadline.
'Is finishing' is the present continuous and describes an action in progress now.
'Has finished' is the present perfect, which connects a past action to the present.
'Would finish' is the conditional form used for hypothetical situations.

questions.explanation: 'By next June' points to a deadline in the future, which is expressed with 'will' plus the base form.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the correct option: 'I think it ___ (rain) later this evening.'
questions.context: A small group guessing about the weather in San Salvador, SV.

options.feedback: 'Rains' is the present simple, which would express a general pattern instead.
'Is raining' is the present continuous and describes rain happening now.
'Rained' is the past simple and cannot describe an evening still to come.
'I think it will rain' is the standard way to give a future opinion or prediction.

questions.explanation: An opinion about a future event uses the future simple 'will' plus the base form after the expression 'I think'.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the correct future perfect question: 'By the time you arrive, ___ I ___ (complete) the report?'
questions.context: A planning message between two students in San Salvador, SV.

options.feedback: 'Have completed' is the present perfect, which links the past to the present.
'Will have completed' is the future perfect, which places the completion before the future moment.
'Do complete' is the present simple and cannot place an action before a future moment.
'Will complete' is the future simple, which does not carry the idea of completion beforehand.

questions.explanation: The future perfect uses 'will have' plus the past participle, and in the question 'will' comes before the subject 'I'.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What is the difference between 'will come' and 'is coming'?
questions.context: A question about tense meaning in an English class in San Salvador, SV.

options.text: The first is a prediction; the second is an arrangement already made.
options.feedback: 'Will' presents a future event, while 'is coming' presents a plan fixed in advance.

options.text: Both describe exactly the same kind of event.
options.feedback: One is a plain future and the other is a prearranged plan, so they differ in nuance.

options.text: The first is past and the second is present.
options.feedback: Neither clause sits in the past, so the difference is not one of past versus present.

options.text: The first is a question and the second is a statement.
options.feedback: Both are declarative clauses; only their tense and arrangement meaning differ.

questions.explanation: 'Will come' is a future simple statement or prediction, while 'is coming' is a present continuous that can show an arrangement already made.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the correct option: 'We ___ (meet) at noon, so bring your notebook.'
questions.context: A reminder message sent before a study session in San Salvador, SV.

options.feedback: 'Meet' with no auxiliary is the present simple, which does not signal a future arrangement.
'Will meet' is also possible, but 'are meeting' better expresses a plan already fixed.
'Are meeting' presents a prearranged future appointment as a settled plan.
'Met' is the past simple and would mean the meeting had already happened.

questions.explanation: A fixed arrangement made in advance takes the present continuous, so 'are meeting' is the correct choice here.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the correct auxiliary: 'She ___ (not / want) to go to the concert.'
questions.context: A conversation about weekend plans in a school in San Salvador, SV.

options.feedback: 'Do' goes with 'I', 'you', 'we' and 'they', not with the singular 'she'.
'Does not want' is the third person present simple negative, as required by 'she'.
'Did not want' is the past simple negative and describes a past state.
The negation must follow the auxiliary, so a bare 'not' before the verb is wrong.

questions.explanation: A statement about what someone wants at the moment uses the present simple negative 'does not want', where 'does' carries the negation.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Identify the only grammatical sentence about a future arrangement.
questions.context: An exercise on future tenses in a secondary school in San Salvador, SV.

options.feedback: 'Will arrive' joins the auxiliary with the base form, which is correct.
'Will' cannot be followed by the -ing form of the verb.
'Arrives' is the third person present simple and does not follow 'will'.

options.text: They are will arrive on Friday.
options.feedback: Two auxiliaries cannot govern the same main verb in English.

questions.explanation: Only the sentence built with 'will' plus the base form of the verb is a grammatical future simple.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the correct option: 'I promise I ___ (call) you tomorrow.'
questions.context: A promise made to a friend in San Salvador, SV.

options.feedback: 'Am calling' is the present continuous and describes an action happening now.
'Called' is the past simple and would state that the call already happened.
'I promise I will call' is the standard future simple used to make a promise.
'Would' must be followed by the base form 'call', not by the past form 'called'.

questions.explanation: A promise made at the moment of speaking uses the future simple 'will' plus the base form.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the correct option to complete the sentence: 'When I finish my homework, I ___ to the park.'
questions.context: An after-school plan described in a school in San Salvador, SV.

options.feedback: 'Go' with no auxiliary is the present simple and gives the sentence an unfinished feel.
'Am going' is the present continuous, which would suggest the plan is already underway.
'Went' is the past simple and cannot follow 'when I finish'.
'Will go' is the future simple main clause that follows the future time clause.

questions.explanation: 'When I finish' is a future time clause, and the main clause usually follows with the future simple 'will go'.
questions.subject: ingles
